Power analysis for sc-ExWAS study design

Source: R/power.R
estimate_power.Rd

Approximates the power to detect a donor-level exposure effect on one gene in one cell type at the pseudobulk level, for a range of donor numbers.

Usage

estimate_power(
  n_donors = seq(10, 100, by = 10),
  effect_size = 0.5,
  n_genes = 5000L,
  n_celltypes = 5L,
  alpha = 0.05,
  dispersion = 0.1,
  base_mean = 100,
  exposure_sd = 1
)

Arguments

n_donors

Integer vector. Donor sample sizes to evaluate. Default: seq(10, 100, by = 10).

effect_size

Numeric. Expected log2 fold change per unit exposure. Default 0.5.

n_genes

Integer. Number of genes tested (for multiple testing correction). Default 5000.

n_celltypes

Integer. Number of cell types tested. Default 5.

alpha

Numeric. Family-wise significance level; the per-test level is alpha / (n_genes * n_celltypes). Default 0.05.

dispersion

Numeric. Negative-binomial dispersion \(\phi\) of donor pseudobulk counts, whose variance is \(\mu + \phi\mu^2\). Default 0.1.

base_mean

Numeric. Mean donor pseudobulk count \(\mu\) of the gene. Default 100; Inf gives the large-count limit.

exposure_sd

Numeric. Standard deviation of the exposure variable across donors. Default 1 (standardised). For a binary exposure that a proportion \(q\) of the donors have, the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{q(1 - q)}\), 0.5 for two groups of equal size; effect_size is then the log2 fold change between the groups.

Value

A DataFrame with columns: n_donors, power, effect_size, exposure_sd, n_tests, alpha_adjusted, dispersion, base_mean.

Details

For a negative-binomial GLM with a log link, the large-sample standard error of the exposure coefficient on the \(\log_2\) scale is $$SE = \frac{\sqrt{1/\mu + \phi}}{\log(2)\, s_x \sqrt{n}},$$ where \(s_x\) is exposure_sd and \(n\) the number of donors. Power is that of a two-sided Wald test at the Bonferroni per-test level. The approximation treats the dispersion as known and uses the normal distribution, so it is optimistic for small numbers of donors; simulate from the planned design when an accurate figure matters. Bonferroni is conservative relative to Benjamini-Hochberg control of the false discovery rate.

Pseudobulk inference has donors, not cells, as its independent units. More cells per donor raise \(\mu\) and so shrink the \(1/\mu\) term, but they do not increase \(n\).

References

Squair JW et al. (2021). Confronting false discoveries in single-cell differential expression. Nat Commun 12:5692.

Examples

pw <- estimate_power(n_donors = seq(10, 50, by = 10),
    effect_size = 0.5, n_genes = 2000, n_celltypes = 3)
pw
#> DataFrame with 5 rows and 8 columns
#>    n_donors     power effect_size exposure_sd   n_tests alpha_adjusted

#> 4        40  0.984320         0.5           1      6000    8.33333e-06
#> 5        50  0.998319         0.5           1      6000    8.33333e-06
#>   dispersion base_mean
